brief_context: Location of the London Branch of the E.A.W. conference.
article_title: HOLD ON TO THE HIGHER STANDARDS
brief_extract: W. Dale, of the British Electrical Development Association, at the One-Day Conference organised by the London Branch of the E.A.W. on November 8th.

location_standardised: England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Mentioned in the context of the Garden Cities of England.
article_title: HOLD ON TO THE HIGHER STANDARDS
brief_extract: The past few years have seen the introduction of electricity to the countryside, and a resultant new way of living, which combines the amenities of city life with the freedom and freshness of rural surroundings. Progressive women will encourage the development of electricity, especially in the evacuation reception areas, so that the emigrants from the cities may appreciate to the full this higher plane of life; the period after the war will see, instead of the crowded populations of the highly urbanised centres, the establishment of the principles of the Garden Cities of England. THE BEST OF BOTH WORLDS.

article_title: TWO GREAT PERSONALITIES PASS AWAY — BOTH FRIENDS OF THE E.A.W. THE ELECTRICAL PIONEER — THE WOMAN DOCTOR
brief_extract: The E.A.W. passed five happy and vigorous years above the Kensington and Knightsbridge Electric Lighting Company, Colonel Crompton's first station of any importance in England, and his interest and friendship did much to establish the future success of the Association. A Yorkshireman, he was a naval cadet in the Crimea, a soldier, he trained electrical engineers in the South African War, and was engaged in tank design during the Great War, besides being responsible for the mechanisation of the Army while in India; a great inventor, a manufacturer and installation contractor, a Government official, a lecturer and able exponent of the electrical principles which fascinated him—these are all facets of his many-sided genius.

brief_extract: The daughter of a Glasgow physician and married to Mr. Stennett Chesser, of Edinburgh, Elizabeth Sloan Chesser gained an early and penetrating realisation of social problems during her medical training at Queen Margaret College and the Royal Infirmary, Glasgow. article_title: WINNING THE WAR IN THE KITCHEN
brief_extract:
REPLANS ITS WORKING KITCHEN
FOR THE NATIONAL SERVICE OF HOUSECRAFT

WINNING the war in the kitchen! This would seem a strange saying to the crossbowmen of Crecy, the sailors of Trafalgar, or even the combatants of Waterloo, who had left their womenfolk behind. To-day, however, there are many more factors in winning this war, and we are conscious that the issue of the present struggle depends no less on the Home Front than on the conduct in other spheres.

H. Mottram,
Professor of Physiology in the University of London
(King's College of Household and Social Science), gave

was concerned with science as applied to everyday life,

location_standardised: Toronto, Ontario, Canada
brief_context: City where Professor Mottram saw his ideas in practice.
brief_extract:
Mr. Howard Marshall, the well-known broadcaster,
and now of the Ministry of Food, was among the guests,
who also included some Canadian soldiers, who were
interested in Professor Mottram's statement that he had
to go to Toronto to see some of his ideas put into
practice. NOT NECESSARY TO BE WELL-OFF TO
BE WELL

This was Professor Mottram's main text, coupled with
the statement that "Feeding the people in wartime is
only a continuance of feeding them in peace time." He
mentioned several analyses comparing family incomes
with nutritive diet, making special reference to investi-
gations of Sir John Orr and David Lubbock, and Sir
William Crawford.

location_standardised: Great Britain, United Kingdom
